card.signals: "contains duplicate", "find pair/triplet summing to X", "group by property", "count frequency", "subarray sum equals K", "longest sequence".
card.core: Trade space for time — a hash map/set turns O(n2) lookups into O(1); prefix sums turn "range sum" questions into O(1) queries after O(n) preprocessing.
card.complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space for hashing; O(n) time O(1) space for Kadane- style scans.
card.traps: Forgetting to handle duplicates/negatives in prefix sums; using a map when sorting + two pointers would avoid extra space; off-by-one errors in prefix-sum ranges.

card.signals: sorted array, "pair/triplet summing to target", palindrome check, partitioning, "remove duplicates in place", merging two sorted structures.
card.core: two indices moving toward each other (opposite-direction) or in the same direction at different speeds shrink the search space from O(n2) to O(n), usually after sorting.
card.complexity: O(n log n) if sorting is required, else O(n); O(1) extra space.

card.signals: "contiguous subarray/substring", longest/shortest such that condition holds, "at most K distinct", "exactly K", repeating character constraints.
card.core: maintain a window [left, right] ; expand right greedily, shrink left only when the window violates a constraint, tracking a running aggregate (count map, sum) incrementally instead of recomputing.
card.complexity: O(n) — each pointer moves forward at most n times.

card.signals: sorted (or rotated-sorted) array, "find target/insertion point", "minimize/maximize the answer subject to a feasibility check", matrix with sorted rows/cols.
card.core: repeatedly halve a monotonic search space. Two flavors: (1) search for an exact value/boundary in sorted data, (2) "binary search on the answer" — guess a value, use a feasibility function to decide which half to keep.
card.complexity: O(log n) per search; O(n log n) if binary search is applied per element.

card.signals: "reverse a list", "detect a cycle", "find the middle", "merge sorted lists", "remove Nth node", problems mentioning ListNode .
card.core: pointer manipulation with careful handling of next references; fast/slow pointers solve middle-finding and cycle-detection in one pass; dummy head nodes simplify edge cases (empty list, removing head).
card.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space for most; recursion trades O(1) space for O(n) call stack.

card.signals: "valid parentheses/expression", "next greater/smaller element", histogram/skyline problems, "daily temperatures", undo/backtrack-style processing, expression evaluation.
card.core: a stack naturally models nested/LIFO structure (matching brackets, recursive expressions). A monotonic stack (kept increasing or decreasing) lets you find, for every element, the nearest greater/smaller neighbor in O(n) total instead of O(n2).
card.complexity: O(n) — each element pushed/popped at most once.

card.signals: level-order traversal (BFS), "sliding window maximum/minimum", task scheduling with cooldowns, anything processed in FIFO arrival order.
card.core: a queue models FIFO/level-by-level processing; a deque used as a "monotonic queue" maintains window extrema in O(1) amortized per operation by discarding elements that can never become the answer.
card.complexity: O(n) — each element enters/leaves the queue once.

card.signals: "generate all subsets/permutations/combinations", "find all valid arrangements satisfying constraints", grid path exploration, N-Queens-style placement.
card.core: explore a decision tree by making a choice, recursing, then undoing the choice (backtrack) to try the next option. Pruning invalid branches early is what makes it tractable.
card.complexity: exponential in the worst case (O(2^n) subsets, O(n!) permutations) — the goal is correct pruning, not beating the theoretical bound.

card.signals: anything with TreeNode , "binary search tree," "path sum," "lowest common ancestor," "serialize/deserialize," "diameter/height," tree construction from traversals.
card.core: most tree problems reduce to DFS (pre/in/post-order) or BFS (level order), often by defining a recursive function that returns information to its parent (height, whether a property holds, etc.) — "think about what one call should return, then trust the recursion."
card.complexity: O(n) time, O(h) recursion stack (h = height; O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed).

card.signals: "Kth largest/smallest", "top K", "merge K sorted", "median of a stream," scheduling by priority, "closest K points."
card.core: a heap keeps the min (or max) accessible in O(1) with O(log n) insert/remove — ideal whenever you repeatedly need "the current best/worst" without full sorting. A "two heaps" (max-heap for lower half, min-heap for upper half) pattern maintains a running median.
card.complexity: O(n log k) for top-K-style problems (much better than O(n log n) full sort when k ≪ n).

card.signals: explicit graph/adjacency list, grid problems ("number of islands", "shortest path in a grid"), "prerequisite" / ordering problems, "connected components," anything mentioning cities/flights/dependencies.
card.core: represent the graph (adjacency list/matrix, or implicit grid), then apply BFS (shortest path in unweighted graphs, level-by-level spread), DFS (reachability, cycle detection, connected components), Union-Find (dynamic connectivity), topological sort (ordering with dependencies), or Dijkstra (weighted shortest path).
card.complexity: O(V+E) for BFS/DFS; O(E log V) for Dijkstra with a heap; O(E· α (V)) ≈ O(E) for Union-Find with path compression.

card.signals: "count the number of ways," "min/max cost to reach," "can you partition/reach a target," overlapping subproblems visible in a naive recursive solution, optimal substructure ("the best solution to the whole uses the best solution to a smaller piece").
card.core: define a recurrence relating a subproblem to smaller subproblems, memoize (top- down) or tabulate (bottom-up) to avoid recomputation. The real skill is defining the state (what varies?) and the transition (how does one state relate to others?) — not the coding itself.
card.complexity: O(states × transition cost) — commonly O(n), O(n2), or O(n·k) depending on state dimensions.

card.signals: "minimum number of X to achieve Y," interval scheduling, "can you reach the end," problems where a locally-optimal choice provably never hurts the global answer.
card.core: make the locally best choice at each step and never reconsider it — valid only when you can prove an exchange argument (swapping any other choice for the greedy one never makes things worse). Sorting is almost always step 1.
card.complexity: O(n log n) (dominated by the initial sort).

card.signals: arrays of [start, end] pairs, "merge overlapping," "insert a new meeting," "minimum rooms needed," calendar/scheduling wording.
card.core: sort intervals by start (for merging) or track boundaries with a sweep-line (for counting overlaps at any point). Two intervals overlap iff a.start < b.end and b.start < a.end .
card.complexity: O(n log n), dominated by sorting.

card.signals: "without using +/-", "find the single/missing number," "count set bits," subsets via bitmask, "power of two/four" checks, XOR-heavy wording.
card.core: XOR cancels identical values ( a^a=0 , a^0=a ) making it ideal for "find the odd one out" problems; n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit (useful for counting bits or checking powers of two); a bitmask can represent a subset of up to ~20-ish items compactly for DP- over-subsets.
card.complexity: O(1) per operation, O(32) or O(64) for full-integer bit scans, O(n·2^n) for bitmask DP over n items.

card.signals: primes, GCD/LCM, modular arithmetic ("answer modulo 10^9+7"), combinatorics counting, "power" computation, digit manipulation.
card.core: most interview math reduces to a handful of reusable tools — Euclidean algorithm for GCD, Sieve of Eratosthenes for prime enumeration, fast exponentiation for large powers, and modular arithmetic identities to keep numbers bounded.
card.complexity: O(log(min(a,b))) for GCD, O(n log log n) for sieve, O(log n) for fast exponentiation.

card.signals: "prefix," "autocomplete," "word dictionary with wildcard search," "longest common prefix of many strings," XOR-maximization over a set of numbers.
card.core: a trie (prefix tree) shares common prefixes across many strings in a tree structure, giving O(L) insert/search (L = string length) regardless of how many strings are stored — far better than storing all strings in a set for prefix-based queries.
card.complexity: O(L) per insert/search where L is the word length; O(N·L) to build from N words.

card.signals: "range sum/min/max query with updates" (mutable range queries), "count of smaller elements after self," "k-th order statistic with updates," anything requiring both point updates AND range queries efficiently.
card.core: plain prefix sums/arrays are O(1) query but O(n) update; a Segment Tree or Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree) achieves O(log n) for both point updates and range queries — the standard structure whenever both are required together.
card.complexity: O(log n) per update/query; O(n) or O(n log n) to build.

details.pattern: Hashing / Set membership.
details.concept: use a hash set to detect repeats in one pass.
details.why: the simplest possible "trade space for time" problem; sets the mental model for everything else in this section.
details.approach: iterate, insert into set, return true if already present.
details.insight: sorting also works in O(n log n) with O(1) space — know both trade-offs.
details.mistake: using nested loops (O(n2)) under time pressure.
details.variation: "contains duplicate within distance k" (sliding window + set).

details.pattern: Hashing / Frequency map.
details.concept: character frequency counting.
details.why: frequency-map pattern reused constantly in string problems.
details.approach: count chars in one string, decrement using the other, check all zero.
details.insight: sorting both strings and comparing is a simpler O(n log n) alternative.
details.mistake: ignoring Unicode/case sensitivity assumptions.
details.variation: Group Anagrams (#4).

details.pattern: Hashing / Complement lookup.
details.concept: store value→index while scanning, check for complement.
details.why: the canonical interview warm-up; complement-lookup generalizes to 3Sum, 4Sum, subarray-sum problems.
details.approach: single pass hash map of seen values to index.
details.insight: only need one pass because you check-then-insert.
details.mistake: using the same element twice; returning values instead of indices.
details.variation: Two Sum II (sorted array → two pointers), Two Sum BST.

details.pattern: Hashing / Canonical key.
details.concept: map each string to a canonical signature (sorted string or 26-count tuple) and bucket by it.
details.why: teaches the "canonical key" trick used across many grouping problems.
details.approach: hash map of signature → list of strings.
details.insight: counting-based signature (O(n)) beats sorting-based signature (O(n log n)) for large inputs.
details.mistake: using sorted string as key when a count-array key would be faster.
details.variation: Group Shifted Strings.

details.pattern: Hashing + Heap / Bucket sort.
details.concept: count frequencies, then either a heap of size K or bucket sort by frequency.
details.why: bridges Arrays & Hashing into the Heap topic; bucket sort gives O(n) which impresses interviewers.
details.approach: frequency map → bucket array indexed by frequency → read off top K.
details.insight: bucket sort avoids the O(n log k) heap cost entirely.
details.mistake: defaulting to sort-everything O(n log n) without mentioning the O(n) bucket approach.
details.variation: Top K Frequent Words (tie-break lexicographically).

details.pattern: Prefix/Suffix products.
details.concept: precompute prefix product and suffix product without division.
details.why: the classic "no division allowed" constraint forces the prefix/suffix pattern used broadly in DP and array problems.
details.approach: left-to-right prefix array, right-to-left suffix pass multiplied into the same output array for O(1) extra space.
details.insight: you can do it in a single output array reused as both prefix and suffix storage.
details.mistake: using division and not handling zeros correctly.
details.variation: same with a zero in the array.

details.pattern: Hashing / Matrix traversal.
details.concept: encode (row, col, box) constraints as hash set keys.
details.why: teaches multi-dimensional constraint hashing seen again in matrix problems.
details.approach: three sets of sets (rows, cols, boxes) keyed by index, encode box index as (r/3, c/3).
details.insight: a single set with composite keys like "r5#3" avoids needing three separate structures.
details.mistake: forgetting box index formula.
details.variation: Sudoku Solver (backtracking).

details.pattern: Hashing / Sequence detection.
details.concept: only start counting a sequence from its true starting number (num-1 not in set).
details.why: teaches the "skip unless start of run" trick that appears in interval/graph problems too.
details.approach: put all numbers in a set, for each number check if num-1 absent, then count forward.
details.insight: this achieves O(n) despite looking like nested loops, because inner loops only execute for true sequence starts.
details.mistake: not checking the "is this a start" condition, causing O(n2).
details.variation: longest consecutive sequence in a binary tree.

details.pattern: Prefix sum + Hashing.
details.concept: store frequency of prefix sums seen so far; subarray sum = prefixSum[j] - prefixSum[i].
details.why: the gateway problem for the entire "prefix sum + hash map" family (divisible by K, equal 0/1 count, etc.).
details.approach: running prefix sum, look up prefixSum - k in a frequency map, increment count.
details.insight: initialize map with {0:1} to count subarrays starting at index 0.
details.mistake: forgetting the {0:1} seed value, undercounting valid subarrays.
details.variation: Subarray Sums Divisible by K (#14), Contiguous Array (equal 0s/1s).

details.pattern: Prefix sum + Modulo hashing.
details.concept: two indices with the same prefix-sum-mod-k imply the subarray between them is divisible by k.
details.why: reinforces modular-arithmetic + prefix-sum combination.
details.approach: store first-seen index of each remainder; check for gap ≥ 2.
details.insight: store the index , not the count, since only the earliest occurrence maximizes subarray length.
details.mistake: mishandling the length ≥ 2 requirement and negative-mod languages.
details.variation: Subarray Sums Divisible by K.

details.pattern: Dynamic Programming (1D) / Greedy.
details.concept: at each index decide whether to extend the previous subarray or start fresh.
details.why: Kadane's is the entry point to 1D DP thinking — "extend vs restart" recurs throughout DP.
details.approach: cur = max(num, cur+num) , track global max.
details.insight: the moment cur drops below 0 it can never help a future sum.
details.mistake: initializing global max to 0 instead of -infinity (fails on all-negative arrays).
details.variation: return the subarray itself; Maximum Circular Subarray.

details.pattern: Dynamic Programming (1D).
details.concept: track both running max AND running min, since a negative number can flip min into max.
details.why: teaches "track two DP states" when a single running value isn't sufficient.
details.approach: at each step compute candidates (num, maxSoFar num, minSoFar num); new max/min are the extremes of those three.
details.insight: swap max/min trackers whenever num is negative, before updating (or compute both, then pick).
details.mistake: only tracking max and losing the sign-flip case.
details.variation: max product of two/three numbers (no DP).

details.pattern: Prefix sum.
details.concept: precompute prefix sums once, answer queries in O(1).
details.why: the textbook intro to prefix sums before jumping to 2D or DP contexts.
details.approach: prefix[i] = prefix[i-1] + nums[i-1] ; range sum = prefix[r+1]-prefix[l] .
details.insight: pad prefix array with a leading 0 to avoid edge-case branching.
details.mistake: off-by-one in inclusive ranges.
details.variation: Range Sum Query 2D, Range Sum Query Mutable (Fenwick Tree).

details.pattern: Prefix sum + Modulo hashing.
details.concept: identical to #9 but keyed by remainder instead of raw sum.
details.why: cements the prefix-sum-hashing generalization (works for equality, modulo, or any invariant).
details.approach: hash map of remainder frequency, handle negative remainders with ((r % k) + k) % k .
details.insight: negative modulo handling is the main gotcha across languages.
details.mistake: not normalizing negative remainders.
details.variation: none beyond #9/#10.

details.pattern: Array as Hash Table (in-place).
details.concept: place each value v at index v-1 via swapping, then scan for the first mismatch.
details.why: the flagship "use the array itself as a hash set" trick for O(1) space, a favorite MAANG hard.
details.approach: cyclic sort — swap nums[i] to nums[nums[i]-1] while in range and not already correct; then find first index where nums[i] != i+1 .
details.insight: answer is always in [1, n+1] , bounding the search space.
details.mistake: infinite loop from mishandling duplicate/self-swaps.
details.variation: Find All Duplicates in an Array (same cyclic-sort trick).

details.pattern: Hashing + Array design.
details.concept: combine a hash map (value→index) with a dynamic array to get O(1) insert/delete/random-access.
details.why: a design problem that tests whether hashing intuition extends beyond lookups to full data-structure design.
details.approach: on delete, swap the target with the last array element before popping, and update the map.
details.insight: "swap-with-last-then-pop" avoids O(n) shifting on delete.
details.mistake: forgetting to update the map index for the swapped element.
details.variation: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) - Duplicates allowed.

details.pattern: Opposite-direction pointers on sorted input.
details.concept: move left pointer up if sum too small, right pointer down if too large.
details.why: as the template for 3Sum/4Sum.
details.approach: two pointers from both ends.
details.insight: sortedness is what makes monotonic pointer movement correct.
details.mistake: not realizing input is 1-indexed in LeetCode's version.
details.variation: 3Sum, 4Sum.

details.pattern: Sort + fix one element + two pointers on the rest.
details.concept: reduce 3-variable search to 2-variable via sorting and fixing.
details.why: as one of the most- asked MAANG mediums, and the template for k-Sum generalization.
details.approach: sort array; for each i, two-pointer search for pairs summing to -nums[i] ; skip duplicate i and duplicate pair values.
details.insight: the "skip duplicates" logic must run on both the outer loop and the inner pointers.
details.mistake: producing duplicate triplets.
details.variation: 4Sum, 3Sum Smaller, k-Sum general recursion.

details.pattern: Opposite-direction pointers with a greedy "move the shorter wall" rule.
details.concept: moving the taller wall can never increase area since width shrinks and height is capped by the shorter wall.
details.why: as proof that two- pointer greedy reasoning generalizes beyond sum problems.
details.approach: start at both ends, always move the pointer at the shorter height inward.
details.insight: this greedy step is provably safe — a classic exchange argument.
details.mistake: moving both pointers or the taller one.
details.variation: Trapping Rain Water.

details.pattern: Two pointers tracking running max height from both sides.
details.concept: water above index i = min(maxLeft, maxRight) - height[i].
details.why: as one of the most iconic hard problems, testable via two pointers, DP (precomputed max arrays), or monotonic stack — knowing all three shows depth.
details.approach: two pointers with leftMax/rightMax; advance the side with the smaller max, since that side's water level is determined.
details.insight: you never need the global max, only the smaller of the two current maxes.
details.mistake: trying to compute exact height contribution without realizing the min(leftMax,rightMax) trick.
details.variation: Trapping Rain Water II (2D, heap-based).

details.pattern: Implicit sliding window / single pass min-tracking.
details.concept: track minimum price seen so far, compute profit at each step.
details.why: as the easiest gateway into "single pass with running state" thinking.

details.pattern: Variable window + frequency/last-seen map.
details.concept: shrink window whenever a repeat is found by jumping left pointer past the previous occurrence.
details.why: as the definitive variable-window template.

details.mistake: using a naive shrink loop instead of the O(1) jump (still correct but less optimal to explain).

details.pattern: Fixed-size window + frequency map comparison.
details.concept: slide a window the size of s1 across s2, compare frequency counts.
details.why: as the template for "does a fixed-size window match a target multiset" problems.

details.pattern: Monotonic deque.

details.mistake: using a max-heap (O(n log n), works but suboptimal) instead of a deque.

details.pattern: Binary search on the answer with a feasibility check.

details.pattern: Doubly linked list + hash map design.

details.pattern: Post-order recursion returning the best downward path from a node, while tracking a global max that may bend through the node (left+right+val).
details.why: as one of the most important hard tree problems — combines #93's "track global while returning a different local value" pattern with negative-number handling.
details.approach: helper returns max(0, val + max(leftGain, rightGain)) (clamping negative contributions to 0); global max updated with val + leftGain + rightGain at every node.
details.insight: a path returned upward to the parent can only include one side (can't fork), but the global answer may fork at any node — this distinction is the crux of the problem.
details.mistake: returning the "forked" sum upward instead of just one branch, corrupting the parent's calculation.

details.pattern: Min-heap of size k, or Quickselect for O(n) average.

details.pattern: Two heaps — a max-heap for the lower half, a min-heap for the upper half, kept balanced in size.

details.pattern: Multi-source DFS/BFS from both ocean borders, reversed flow direction, then intersect reachable sets.
details.concept: instead of checking "can water from this cell reach the ocean" (expensive per-cell), reverse the question to "which cells can the ocean reach flowing uphill," starting BFS from all border cells simultaneously.

details.approach: two separate multi-source BFS/DFS runs (one per ocean) using the reversed "can flow uphill into me" condition; answer is the intersection of both visited sets.
details.insight: reversing the traversal direction turns an O(cells × traversal) brute force into two O(cells) passes.
details.mistake: attempting per-cell traversal to each ocean (very slow, TLE on large grids).

Approach: color each component alternately as you traverse; if a neighbor is already the same color as the current node, return false. Insight: must check every connected component separately (graph may be disconnected). Mistake: forgetting disconnected components, or not properly propagating alternating colors. details.pattern: BFS over an implicit graph where edges connect words differing by one letter.
details.concept: treat each word as a graph node; BFS finds the shortest transformation sequence since BFS naturally finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
details.why: as a flagship "recognize the implicit graph" hard problem — the graph is never given explicitly, which is the real challenge.
details.approach: BFS from beginWord , at each step try changing every letter position to every other letter, checking membership in the word set; level count = transformation length.
details.insight: precomputing wildcard patterns ( h*t for "hot") in a map lets you find neighbors in O(word length) instead of O(dictionary size), critical for passing time limits.
details.mistake: naive O(dictionary size) neighbor lookup per word, causing TLE on large dictionaries.

details.pattern: Dijkstra's algorithm from a single source on a weighted directed graph.
details.why: as the canonical intro to Dijkstra, a must-know weighted- shortest-path algorithm.
details.approach: min-heap of (distance, node) , relax edges, track visited/finalized nodes; answer is the max finalized distance (or -1 if unreachable nodes remain).
details.insight: Dijkstra only works correctly with non-negative weights — always state this assumption explicitly in interviews.
details.mistake: applying Dijkstra to a graph with negative weights (needs Bellman-Ford instead).

details.pattern: Modified Bellman-Ford (or Dijkstra with a stop-count dimension in state).
details.concept: since Dijkstra's greedy finalization doesn't account for a "stops" constraint, use Bellman-Ford relaxation limited to k+1 rounds, or Dijkstra with state (cost, node, stopsUsed) .
details.why: as a great example of a standard algorithm needing modification for an added constraint — testing algorithmic adaptability, not just memorization.
details.approach: Bellman-Ford-style — relax all edges k+1 times using a snapshot of the previous round's distances (to avoid using an edge relaxed in the same round twice).
details.insight: standard Dijkstra's "finalize once visited" assumption breaks with a stops constraint, since a costlier-but-fewer-stops path might matter — this subtlety is the core lesson.
details.mistake: applying vanilla Dijkstra and getting wrong answers on the stops constraint.

details.pattern: Dijkstra-like approach (or binary search + BFS) minimizing the maximum elevation along a path.
details.concept: this is a "minimize the max edge/node weight on a path" problem, solved by a modified Dijkstra using a min-heap keyed on the max-so-far value instead of cumulative sum.
details.why: as an advanced variant showing Dijkstra generalizes beyond simple sum-of-weights shortest paths.

details.pattern: Build a graph of letter-precedence constraints from adjacent word comparisons, then topological sort.
details.concept: compare adjacent words in the sorted list to infer a comes before b edges; topologically sort the resulting letter graph.
details.why: as a hard problem combining graph construction (a non-trivial step) with topological sort (#120/#121).
details.approach: for each adjacent word pair, find the first differing character and add a directed edge; run topological sort (Kahn's or DFS); detect invalid cases (cycle, or a word being a prefix of an earlier word which is invalid ordering).
details.insight: constructing the graph correctly (only from the first differing character between adjacent words, and validating the prefix-invalid case) is the trickiest part, not the topological sort itself.
details.mistake: comparing all pairs of words instead of only adjacent ones, or missing the invalid-prefix edge case.

problems.title: Min Cost to Connect All Points

details.pattern: Minimum Spanning Tree via Prim's or Kruskal's algorithm.
details.concept: connect all points with minimum total edge weight without forming cycles — the classic MST definition.
details.why: as the canonical MST introduction problem.
details.prereqs: #123 (Union-Find) for Kruskal's, or heap basics for Prim's.
details.approach: generate all edges (Manhattan distances), sort by weight, union-find to add edges without creating cycles.
details.insight: Prim's is usually faster here since the graph is dense (all pairs of points are potential edges — O(n2) edges), making Kruskal's sort step expensive; Prim's with a heap avoids ever materializing all edges explicitly.
details.mistake: using Kruskal's naively on a dense graph without considering the edge-generation cost.

details.pattern: Eulerian-path-style DFS (Hierholzer's algorithm) using all edges exactly once, sorted lexicographically.
details.concept: greedily visit the lexicographically smallest next airport, backtracking (via post-order append) when stuck to guarantee all edges are used.
details.why: as an advanced graph-traversal problem requiring awareness of Eulerian paths, less common but a strong differentiator.
details.approach: build adjacency lists sorted lexicographically (as min-heaps or sorted lists), DFS using each edge once, appending nodes to the result in post-order , then reverse.
details.insight: the "append in post-order, then reverse" trick is what correctly handles dead-ends requiring backtracking — this is exactly Hierholzer's algorithm for Eulerian paths.
details.mistake: trying a purely greedy forward DFS without post-order reversal, which fails on itineraries requiring backtracking.

details.pattern: 2D DP over pattern and text, with special handling for . and * .
details.concept: * means "zero or more of the preceding element," requiring a DP transition that considers both "use the * to match nothing" and "use it to match one more occurrence." Matters as one of the hardest string DP problems, frequently used to separate strong candidates.

details.pattern: Catalan number recurrence — dp[n] = sum(dp[i]*dp[n-1-i]) for i in 0..n-1 .
details.concept: for each choice of root value, the left subtree uses smaller values and the right subtree uses larger ones, and the count of valid trees is independent of which specific values, only how many .

details.approach: bottom-up DP over n , using the recurrence above.

details.mistake: trying to enumerate actual trees (that's Unique BST II — exponential, different problem) instead of just counting.

Approach: build a trie from the word list; DFS from every grid cell, walking both the grid and the trie simultaneously, marking found words and removing them from the trie to avoid duplicate detection. details.why: as a clever, less obvious application of tries beyond strings — bitwise tries for numeric maximization problems.

details.pattern: Fenwick Tree (BIT) or Segment Tree supporting O(log n) point update and O(log n) range sum query.
details.why: as the definitive introduction to why plain prefix sums (#13) fail once updates are introduced, motivating these advanced structures.
details.approach: array indexed by i & -i (lowest set bit) jumps for both update and prefix-sum query.
details.insight: the contrast with #13 is the whole point — a mutable array needs a fundamentally different structure to keep both operations logarithmic; a naive prefix-sum array is O(1) query but O(n) update, which fails under frequent updates.
details.mistake: recomputing prefix sums from scratch after every update (O(n) per update, too slow for many updates).

problems.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

details.pattern: Fenwick Tree over compressed value ranks, processing the array right-to-left (or merge-sort based counting).
details.concept: for each element, count how many smaller elements have been "inserted" into the Fenwick tree so far (processing from the end backward).
details.why: as a genuinely hard application combining coordinate compression with a Fenwick Tree, or alternatively solvable via modified merge sort — both are valuable to know.
details.approach: compress values to ranks, iterate right-to-left, query count of ranks less than current, then insert current rank.
details.insight: coordinate compression (mapping values to their sorted rank) is essential since raw values may be too large/sparse for a direct Fenwick array index.
details.mistake: forgetting to compress coordinates first, causing infeasible array sizes for large value ranges.

details.pattern: Sweep-line + a max-heap (or a balanced multiset/ordered structure) tracking currently active building heights.
details.concept: process building edges (start=add height, end=remove height) in sorted x-order, tracking the current max height at each event, outputting a new skyline point whenever the max height changes.
details.why: as an iconic hard problem combining sweep-line thinking with a heap or ordered-structure for tracking "currently active maximum."
details.prereqs: #175 (sweep-line from Meeting Rooms II), heap fluency.
details.approach: create (x, height, isStart) events, sort them (careful tie-breaking for simultaneous starts/ends), sweep through maintaining a max-heap (with lazy deletion for expired buildings) or a multiset of active heights.
details.insight: correctly breaking ties among simultaneous events (process all starts at an x before ends, and taller starts before shorter ones) is the trickiest correctness detail.
details.mistake: incorrect event ordering/tie-breaking, producing skylines with spurious extra points.

details.pattern: Hash map for scores + sorting (or a Fenwick Tree/ordered structure) for top-K queries.
details.why: as a practical design problem testing whether advanced structures are even necessary (often a hash map + sort suffices at LeetCode's given scale).
details.approach: hash map of player→score; top(K) sorts current scores and sums the top K (acceptable given constraints); a Fenwick Tree over score ranks would optimize this further for very frequent queries.
details.insight: recognizing when a "fancy" advanced structure is overkill relative to given constraints — and being able to articulate the trade- off — is itself a valued interview skill.
details.mistake: over-engineering with a full Fenwick Tree/segment tree when the given constraints make simple sorting perfectly adequate.

details.pattern: Store booked intervals and linearly (or via a sorted structure/segment tree) check for overlap on each new booking.
details.why: as an entry point into "online interval insertion with overlap checking," extendable to segment-tree-based solutions for the harder follow-ups (My Calendar II/III use exactly this same skeleton with added complexity).
details.approach: maintain a sorted list (or simple list, fine at LeetCode's scale) of booked intervals; check newStart < existingEnd and existingStart < newEnd against all others before inserting.
details.insight: the follow-up problems (double/triple booking) naturally motivate moving from a naive O(n) check per booking to a segment tree over compressed time ranges — good to mention proactively.
details.mistake: not recognizing this simple version as a stepping stone toward the segment-tree-required harder variants.
